source.title: Self-paced Data Augmentation for Training Neural Networks
source.authors: Tomoumi Takase; Ryo Karakida; H. Asoh

record.tranche_reason: Tests data augmentation choices in image classifiers across datasets and sample sizes, a setting not covered by the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy and training-loss behavior for self-paced data augmentation (SPA), conventional augmentation (CA), and no augmentation (NA). The optimizer, batch size, model, dataset, augmentation, sample count, and threshold vary across experiments. Cited results about other methods are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests selective data augmentation, which none of V1–V8 names. All experiments use Adam and batch size 100; there are no optimizer, batch-size, width, architecture, dropout, random-label, or memorized-example-removal comparisons. Sections 5.3–5.4 discuss sharp minima but measure minibatch-loss variance, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that SPA generally improves performance, especially with limited data or unsuitable augmentation, while full-data benefits are smaller and inconsistent. They interpret the loss dynamics as consistent with curriculum learning and a transition toward stable training; they do not directly establish sharper-versus-flatter minima.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies selective data augmentation based on each sample's training loss, rather than the original claim's tests of random-label memorization, width, architecture, optimizer, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies with training-set size, dataset, augmentation technique, SPA threshold λ, and whether the dataset is full or reduced.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10 with 1,000 samples, SPA achieves 52.78% versus 49.12% for matched-count random augmentation selection. With rotation, SPA achieves 47.72%, above conventional augmentation's 39.33% but below no augmentation's 48.47%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selecting examples for augmentation by training loss can change held-out accuracy, with benefits depending on augmentation and comparison condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmentation raises and destabilizes minibatch training loss. On reduced data, SPA transitions from conventional-augmentation-like to no-augmentation-like loss variance; on full data its variance pattern differs less from the controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selective augmentation changes training-loss dynamics, with different patterns on reduced and full training sets.

record.problems: The paper reports best test accuracy over training rather than a train-test error gap. Several training-loss and variance results are presented as plots without exact numerical values in the text. Five-trial means and standard errors are stated for reduced-data experiments; the full-dataset table does not state uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Many table entries report separate dataset, augmentation, threshold, and sample-count combinations. They are omitted under the 60-row limit, prioritizing an explicit matched-count sample-selection comparison, a condition where SPA exceeds CA but not NA, and training-loss findings. Additional test-accuracy conditions appear in Tables 1–3 and Sections 4.2–4.5; additional loss and variance traces appear in Figures 1, 6–9.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning scope, weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations; batch size is fixed at 100.
Dropout effects, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining, compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: A new experimental setting alone does not warrant T3 when none of the listed versions is tested. Omitted augmentation results are declared in rows_left_out and do not supply tests of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and related tuning effects.
Large versus small batch training and adjustments to training recipes.
Dropout effects and its interaction with weight decay and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: SPA selected samples for augmentation using training-loss threshold λ = 0.1; compared with random selection at the same augmentation count.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors stated in the values.
rows.note: Authors state the number of augmented samples was matched to SPA.
rows.check: The numbers match Section 5.2, but this is the study's own augmentation method compared with random augmentation selection, not evidence for any listed version. Exclude from claim-result rows.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: SPA applied rotation augmentation to samples with training loss greater than λ = 0.1; compared with CA.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors stated in the values.
rows.note: Table 2 lists NA for CIFAR-10 (1k) as 48.47 (±0.49); SPA is higher than CA but lower than NA.
rows.check: The numbers match Table 2, but SPA versus conventional augmentation tests none of V1–V8. Exclude this method-performance comparison from claim-result rows.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: Measured best test accuracy for SPA against no augmentation (NA), with rotation augmentation.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors stated in the values.
rows.note: This comparison shows SPA did not exceed NA in this condition.
rows.check: The numbers match Table 2. Lower SPA accuracy than no augmentation is not a reversal of any listed version. Exclude this method-performance comparison from claim-result rows.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss transitions with and without applying flip and random erasing to all training samples.
rows.value: Training loss increases and changes more significantly for each minibatch than in the no-augmentation case.
rows.note: The paper describes higher and more variable training loss under augmentation; no test error or train-test gap is given for this comparison.
rows.check: Section 5.4 specifies the full CIFAR-10 training set, so training_samples should be 50,000. Higher and more variable minibatch loss under augmentation measures neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor a generalization gap.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared variance in minibatch training loss for SPA, CA, and NA during early and final training stages.
rows.measure: Variance of training loss over training
rows.value: SPA transitions were similar to CA in the early stage and NA in the final stage; the paper states instability changed from unstable to stable.
rows.note: This measures training-loss variance, not a generalization gap.
rows.check: The qualitative description matches Section 5.4, but minibatch-loss variance cannot establish V7's weight-perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps.

rows.subject: small CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared training loss and its minibatch variance under SPA, CA, and NA on the full dataset.
rows.measure: Training loss and variance in training loss
rows.value: SPA training loss was nearly the same as CA in the final stage; its variance trend was similar to CA and NA, and all methods showed large fluctuation.
rows.note: The authors say SPA's effect was small and significant test-accuracy improvements cannot always be expected; this row reports training-loss measurements.
rows.check: The qualitative description matches Figure 9 and Section 5.4. A smaller SPA benefit on full data is not partial evidence for any listed version; loss variance is not magnitude-aware sharpness.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
